result.question: Effects of intermittent fasting and time-restricted eating (TRE) on wearable-trackable physiological metrics — HRV, RHR, sleep, skin/core temperature, respiratory rate, autonomic/stress markers, body composition, exercise performance/VO2max, glucose/insulin sensitivity, and overall recovery/readiness — distinguishing acute (during/right after a fast) from habitual (weeks-to-months) effects, graded by evidence strength, plus safety contraindications and confounds in the wearable signal.

angles.label: broad/primary — systematic reviews & RCTs on IF/TRE cardiometabolic + body composition outcomes
angles.query: time-restricted eating intermittent fasting randomized controlled trial systematic review body composition fat mass insulin sensitivity vs calorie restriction 2018..2025
angles.rationale: Anchors the strongest evidence (items 7, 9) with meta-analyses and RCTs that give effect sizes, sample sizes, and IF-vs-plain-caloric-restriction comparisons — the backbone of the grading.

angles.label: academic/autonomic — HRV, RHR, cortisol and sympatho-vagal balance during and after fasting
angles.query: fasting heart rate variability RMSSD vagal tone cortisol autonomic sympathetic parasympathetic acute overnight fast study
angles.rationale: Directly targets items 1, 2, 6 and 10, and surfaces the acute-vs-habitual split plus the confound that HRV shifts may reflect meal timing/hydration rather than true recovery.

angles.label: sleep & circadian — early vs late TRE, meal timing, hunger and sleep architecture
angles.query: time-restricted eating meal timing sleep quality REM deep sleep architecture early vs late eating hunger circadian randomized trial
angles.rationale: Covers item 3 (and touches temperature/circadian item 4), including whether early TRE beats late eating and how hunger disrupts sleep — a nuanced, confound-prone area.

angles.label: Ramadan natural experiment & athlete performance — VO2max, endurance/strength, temperature, respiration
angles.query: Ramadan fasting athletes VO2max endurance strength performance body temperature respiratory rate systematic review
angles.rationale: Ramadan studies are the largest natural experiment and dominate the athletic/performance literature (items 4, 5, 8); helps distinguish athlete vs sedentary populations and fasted-training effects.

angles.label: safety/contraindications & skeptical — who should not fast, harms, and evidence gaps
angles.query: intermittent fasting contraindications risks eating disorders type 1 diabetes pregnancy underweight adverse effects harms review
angles.rationale: Addresses the safety section (eating-disorder history, pregnancy, T1D, underweight, chronic short sleepers, high training load) and the honest-limitations mandate — where evidence is thin or fasting is contraindicated.

result.summary: Split the question along its two natural axes — the ten physiological metrics and the acute-vs-habitual/evidence-grade dimension — then group metrics by the literature that best serves them: RCT/meta-analytic core for metabolic and body-composition claims, autonomic-physiology studies for HRV/RHR/stress, circadian/sleep trials for sleep and temperature, the Ramadan natural experiment for athletic performance and respiration, and a dedicated safety/skeptical angle for contraindications and evidence gaps.

results.title: The effects of time-restricted eating on sleep in adults: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials (Frontiers in Nutrition, 2024)
results.snippet: Systematic review of RCTs — the strongest evidence tier for item 3. Key honest finding: TRE may improve some sleep-quality aspects in circadian-disrupted populations (e.g. shift workers) but can WORSEN sleep duration/efficiency in others; effects are inconsistent. Ideal anchor for grading TRE-sleep evidence and flagging where it is thin.

results.title: Early but not late time-restricted eating improves actigraphy-estimated sleep quality in women with overweight/obesity — ChronoFast crossover trial (Frontiers in Nutrition, 2026)
results.snippet: Directly answers the early-vs-late TRE angle. Crossover RCT: no between-group difference, but within-group, EARLY TRE (not late) improved sleep efficiency, reduced fragmentation and shortened awakenings. Crucially reports NO association between hunger/satiety and any sleep metric — directly relevant to the 'hunger disrupts sleep' sub-question and confound flagging.

results.title: Effects of Dinner Timing on Sleep Stage Distribution and EEG Power Spectrum in Healthy Volunteers (PMC, 2021)
results.snippet: Randomized study of late dinner (1h before bed) vs routine dinner (5h before bed) with EEG-measured sleep architecture (stages + spectral power) in healthy volunteers. Rare objective look at meal timing effects on REM/deep sleep architecture rather than just self-report/actigraphy — directly supports item 3's architecture and late-eating angle.

results.title: Time-Restricted Eating and Sleep, Mood, and Quality of Life in Adults With Overweight or Obesity: Secondary Analysis of an RCT (PMC / JAMA Netw Open)
results.snippet: RCT secondary analysis on how meal-window timing relates to sleep, mood and QoL — supports the circadian-alignment framing (early eating aligns with circadian rhythm; late eating may blunt sleep/mood benefits). Useful for the habitual-effect and readiness sections.

results.title: Impact of a self-selected time-restricted eating intervention on eating patterns, sleep, and late-night eating in individuals with obesity (PMC)
results.snippet: Real-world self-selected TRE study linking eating patterns and late-night eating to sleep outcomes in obesity. Useful moderate-evidence context on how habitual TRE reshapes late eating and its sleep correlates, and for noting confounds in free-living designs.

results.title: Intended Isocaloric Time-Restricted Eating Shifts Circadian Clocks but Does Not Improve Cardiometabolic Health in Women with Overweight (medRxiv preprint)
results.snippet: ChronoFast-related isocaloric TRE analysis showing meal timing shifts circadian clock phase without cardiometabolic benefit — valuable for the temperature/circadian item 4 crossover and for the honest caveat that circadian phase shifts do not guarantee downstream benefit. Preprint (weaker tier), flag as not peer-reviewed.

results.title: Long-term fasting-induced parasympathetic and sympathetic autonomic nervous system modulation in a subgroup of the GENESIS study (Int J Obes, 2025)
results.snippet: Habitual/prolonged-fasting evidence for items 1, 6, 10. Buchinger protocol (~12 days, ~250 kcal/day), n=16: RMSSD rose from 27.16 to 32.92 ms with reduced sympathetic activity post-fast — supports enhanced vagal tone with sustained fasting. Small sample; supervised extended fast, not everyday TRE — flag as weak/mechanistic. Full text on PMC with DOI to Int J Obes s41366-025-01843-0.

results.title: Solianik & Sedliak et al. — Effects of a 48-h fast on heart rate variability and cortisol levels in healthy female subjects (Eur J Clin Nutr, 2013) [PMID 23403876]
results.snippet: Key ACUTE counter-signal for items 1 and 6: a 48h total fast DECREASED SDNN and RMSSD (parasympathetic withdrawal + sympathetic activation) and shifted the diurnal cortisol slope. Directly supports the acute-vs-habitual split and the app's honesty caveat that a longer fast can look like worse 'recovery.' Verifiable PMID/DOI (ejcn201332).

results.title: Influence of an acute fast on ambulatory blood pressure and autonomic cardiovascular control (Am J Physiol Regul Integr Comp Physiol, 2022)
results.snippet: Acute-fast autonomic/BP evidence for items 2, 6, 10. Controlled crossover examining a single fast's effect on ambulatory BP and cardiovascular autonomic control — useful for RHR/sympatho-vagal balance and for flagging that acute wearable shifts may reflect the fast itself (hydration/hemodynamics) rather than true recovery. PMC12108 open copy available.

results.title: Effect of Intermittent Fasting on Cardiovascular Autonomic Regulation in Healthy Adults
results.snippet: Habitual IF/TRE evidence for items 1, 2, 6: intermittent fasting improved SDNN and RMSSD and reduced resting heart rate, indicating enhanced parasympathetic activity and better autonomic balance over weeks — the habitual counterpart to the acute-withdrawal findings. Confirm study design/sample size before grading (likely moderate).

results.title: GENESIS long-term fasting ANS modulation — publisher version (International Journal of Obesity, Nature, 2025)
results.snippet: Publisher landing page for the GENESIS RMSSD/sympathovagal study — canonical DOI/citation source (author, year, journal) to cite the long-term-fasting HRV figures accurately rather than approximating from the PMC mirror.

results.title: Effects of a 48-h fast on HRV and cortisol in healthy female subjects — full-text PDF (ResearchGate mirror)
results.snippet: Full-text access to the Solianik 48h-fast HRV/cortisol study for pulling exact RMSSD/SDNN and cortisol-slope numbers and the female-only sedentary population detail (sex/population caveat). Use alongside the PubMed/Nature record for the verifiable citation.

results.title: Lowe et al. 2020 — Effects of Time-Restricted Eating on Weight Loss and Other Metabolic Parameters: The TREAT Randomized Clinical Trial (JAMA Internal Medicine)
results.snippet: Landmark 12-week RCT (n=116, overweight/obese adults) directly answering items 7 (body composition) and 8 (lean mass/training). 16:8 TRE produced only modest weight loss (-0.94 kg) vs consistent meal timing, NO significant fat-mass change (-0.51 kg), but a SIGNIFICANT lean-mass loss (-1.10 kg, ~65% of weight lost was lean mass). Primary source with DXA effect sizes — the strongest cautionary evidence that TRE without protein/resistance training risks lean mass. Author/year/journal/DOI all verifiable.

results.title: Trepanowski et al. 2017 — Alternate-Day Fasting vs Daily Calorie Restriction: A Randomized Clinical Trial (JAMA Internal Medicine)
results.snippet: 1-year RCT (n=100 obese adults, 3 arms: ADF, daily CR, control) — the key head-to-head for the IF-vs-plain-calorie-restriction comparison central to grading item 7. ADF produced NO superior weight loss, adherence, or cardiovascular risk improvement vs matched CR; higher dropout in the ADF arm. Directly supports the 'fasting is not magic beyond calorie restriction' framing. Primary RCT with effect sizes and sample size.

results.title: Liu et al. 2022 — Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss (New England Journal of Medicine)
results.snippet: 12-month RCT (n=139, obese adults) isolating the TRE window from calorie restriction: both arms were calorie-restricted, one added an 8-hour window. No significant difference in weight, fat mass, lean mass, waist circumference, glucose, insulin sensitivity, or lipids between TRE+CR and CR alone. The cleanest evidence that TRE benefits are driven by energy restriction, not meal timing per se — essential for honest grading of items 7 and 9.

results.title: 2025 — The impact of intermittent fasting on body composition and cardiometabolic outcomes in overweight and obese adults: systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (PMC)
results.snippet: Recent (2025) meta-analysis pooling RCTs on IF for body composition (item 7) plus cardiometabolic markers relevant to items 2, 9. Provides pooled effect sizes with confidence intervals for weight, fat mass, fat-free mass, glucose, insulin/HOMA-IR, lipids and blood pressure — the strong-evidence backbone for quantitative claims. Useful for stating where pooled effects are significant vs null.

results.title: 2022 — Effects of Time-Restricted Feeding and Ramadan Fasting on Body Weight, Body Composition, Glucose Responses, and Insulin Resistance: A Systematic Review of RCTs (PMC)
results.snippet: Directly covers the Ramadan-fasting natural experiment the question specifically requested, alongside TRE, synthesizing RCTs on weight, body composition, glucose and insulin resistance (items 7, 9). Valuable for distinguishing acute Ramadan-style fasting effects from habitual TRE and for populations beyond sedentary Western cohorts. Systematic-review-grade evidence.

results.title: 2025 — Effects of time-restricted eating on body composition and metabolic parameters in overweight and obese women: systematic review and meta-analysis (Frontiers in Nutrition)
results.snippet: 2025 meta-analysis of 13 RCTs finding TRE significantly reduced body weight and fasting insulin but showed NO significant effect on BMI, fat mass, fat-free mass, visceral fat, glucose, HOMA-IR, lipids or blood pressure. Sex-specific (women) population adds granularity for item 7 and flags how thin/inconsistent the fat-mass and insulin-sensitivity signals are — supports honest 'evidence is mixed' grading.

results.title: Intermittent fasting: consider the risks of disordered eating for your patient (Clinical Diabetes and Endocrinology, 2023)
results.snippet: Peer-reviewed clinical review (full text on PMC, has DOI/PMID) making the core safety case: IF is generally NOT recommended for people with a history of, or risk for, eating disorders because it can exacerbate underlying psychopathology and perpetuate maladaptive patterns. Directly supplies the eating-disorder contraindication section with citable framing for clinicians.

results.title: Ganson et al. 2022 — Intermittent fasting: engagement and associations with eating disorder behaviors among Canadian adolescents and young adults (Eating Behaviors)
results.snippet: The key primary study behind the ED-risk claim (n=2762, ages 16-30). Cross-sectional so evidence is MODERATE/observational (associational, not causal), which honestly flags the limitation. In women, IF associated with overeating, loss of control, binge eating, vomiting, laxative use, compulsive exercise and higher EDE-Q scores; in men with compulsive exercise. Verifiable author/year/journal for the note.

results.title: Sleep Quality and Performance in Professional Athletes Fasting during Ramadan (2021)
results.snippet: Natural-experiment evidence relevant to sleep + high-training-load caution: ~14.6% reduction in sleep performance persisting post-Ramadan, delayed bedtime/wake, increased daytime sleepiness, reduced nocturnal sleep duration, and links between sleep disruption and reduced physical performance. Directly supports the 'chronic short sleepers and high-training-load individuals should be cautious' safety point and the sleep-confound angle.

results.title: The impact of time-restricted eating on health-related quality of life: a systematic literature review (2024)
results.snippet: Systematic review giving the balanced counterpoint: minor self-resolving adverse events (hunger, headache) and no studies showing TRE harmed HR-QoL. Useful for honestly stating that in studied (mostly overweight/metabolic) populations short-term safety is favorable — while noting these trials exclude the vulnerable groups the note flags, so absence of harm signal is population-limited.

results.title: Danger of Intermittent Fasting: Risks, Warnings, and NHS Guidance
results.snippet: Consolidated contraindication list aligned with NHS guidance: pregnant/breastfeeding women, children, frail older adults, ED history, underweight individuals, type 1 diabetes, advanced kidney disease, active cancer. Notes hypoglycaemia risk with insulin/sulphonylureas. Secondary source — use to enumerate contraindicated populations, but trace T1D/pregnancy claims to primary guidance before citing figures.

results.title: Effects of Ramadan intermittent fasting on performance, physiological responses, and bioenergetic pathways during repeated sprint exercise (Frontiers in Nutrition, 2024)
results.snippet: Supports the exercise-performance and readiness-confound sections: performance decrements during Ramadan fasting attributed to dehydration and hypoglycemia rather than training deconditioning — a concrete example of the fast itself (hydration/glycogen state) confounding wearable readiness/performance signals, and a caution flag for high-training-load users.

results.title: Effects of Ramadan Fasting on Physical Performance: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis (Sports Medicine, 2020) — PMID 31960369
results.snippet: The definitive meta-analysis (Cherif/Chtourou et al., Sports Medicine 2020) on the Ramadan natural experiment. Finds most physical performance parameters (aerobic/VO2max, muscle strength, jump height, anaerobic capacity) are NOT significantly affected when normal training is maintained, but Wingate/repeated-sprint mean and peak power ARE degraded, especially in the morning. Directly serves item 8 (endurance vs strength vs sprint) with pooled effect sizes and a citable DOI/PMID.

results.title: Effects of Intermittent Fasting on Specific Exercise Performance Outcomes: A Systematic Review Including Meta-Analysis (Nutrients 2020, 12(5):1390)
results.snippet: Correia et al. meta-analysis distinguishing time-restricted feeding (TRE) from Ramadan IF — key for the acute-vs-habitual and athlete-vs-sedentary framing. Reports VO2max is ENHANCED with TRE protocols but REDUCED with Ramadan fasting, letting the note separate the confound of dehydration/circadian disruption in Ramadan from true training effect. Open-access with full DOI (10.3390/nu12051390).

results.title: Circadian pattern of sleep, energy expenditure, and body temperature of young healthy men during the intermittent fasting of Ramadan (BJN, 2010) — PMID 20100529
results.snippet: Primary source directly covering item 4 (overnight/skin temperature) and item 3 (sleep). Documents a delayed acrophase (phase shift) of skin/body temperature and altered circadian pattern of sleep and energy expenditure during Ramadan — exactly the wearable-tracked temperature and circadian signal, and flags that the wearable signal is confounded by meal-timing/circadian shift rather than recovery.

results.title: Sleep Quality and Performance in Professional Athletes Fasting during the Month of Ramadan (2021) — PMID 34198990
results.snippet: Athlete-population sleep study for item 3 and item 10 (recovery/readiness). Reports ~14.6% reduction in sleep performance during Ramadan that persisted post-Ramadan, plus elevated stress and muscle soreness — grounding claims about sleep architecture disruption, hunger, and impaired recovery in a training population.

results.title: Effect of Ramadan fasting on heart rate variability as a measure of cardiac stress in a Lebanese cohort (Eur J Clin Nutr, 2020) — PMID 31980745
results.snippet: Covers items 1, 2, 6 (HRV, RHR, autonomic/stress). Provides the honest counterpoint the note needs — reports insignificant HRV change between first and last weeks of Ramadan, arguing fasting does not markedly alter cardiac autonomic activity, useful to flag that observed HRV shifts may reflect hydration/meal timing rather than true vagal-tone change.

results.title: Time-Restricted Feeding and Aerobic Performance in Elite Runners: Ramadan Fasting as a Model (Front. Nutrition, 2021)
results.snippet: Elite-endurance study explicitly using Ramadan as a TRE model for item 8. Shows distance-runner aerobic performance can be maintained or slightly improved when sleep and nutrition are optimized and training is modulated — supports the note's caveat that outcomes depend heavily on load management and hydration, not fasting alone.

claims.claim: In a 12-week RCT (N=197 adults with overweight/obesity), adding time-restricted eating (8-hour window) to usual care produced no significant change in sleep quality, sleep efficiency, awakenings, or Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores versus control, regardless of eating-window timing.
claims.quote: incorporating TRE into a UC intervention, regardless of the timing of the eating window, was not associated with significant changes in sleep, mood, or quality of life compared with UC alone.

claims.claim: Early TRE did not increase total sleep time versus control, with a near-zero mean difference of 0.2 hours (95% CI, -0.2 to 0.6).
claims.quote: mean difference in total sleep time, 0.2 [95% CI, –0.2 to 0.6] hours

claims.claim: Neither early nor late 8-hour TRE windows differentially affected sleep, mood, or quality of life outcomes over 12 weeks — early TRE started before 10 AM and late TRE started after 1 PM.
claims.quote: regardless of the timing of the eating window, was not associated with significant changes in sleep, mood, or quality of life

claims.claim: TRE did not worsen mood measures (depression, anxiety, stress) over 12 weeks; early TRE vs control depression score difference was 0.2 points (95% CI, -1.0 to 1.3).
claims.quote: Depression score, 0.2 [95% CI, –1.0 to 1.3] points

claims.claim: In a randomized crossover PSG study of 20 healthy young adults, late dinner (22:00, ~1h before bed) vs routine dinner (18:00, ~5h before bed) did NOT significantly change total sleep time, sleep efficiency, sleep latency, or whole-night sleep-stage distribution — meaning meal timing's effect on overall sleep architecture is modest in healthy young people.
claims.quote: total sleep time, sleep efficiency, sleep latency, as well as whole-night sleep stage distributions were not significantly different

claims.claim: Late dinner produced localized within-night shifts in sleep staging: higher Stage 2 in the second sleep quarter (49.0% vs 36.5%, p=0.0056) and higher REM in the third quarter (28.1% vs 21.9%, p=0.035).
claims.quote: Stage 2 sleep: significantly higher after LD in 2nd quarter (49.0% vs 36.5%, p=0.0056)... REM sleep: significantly higher after LD in 3rd quarter (28.1% vs 21.9%, p=0.035)

claims.claim: EEG spectral analysis showed late dinner increased delta (slow-wave) power by 2.54% at the start of the night while decreasing alpha and beta power, indicating deeper sleep early in the night that then reversed as the night progressed.
claims.quote: LD increased delta power by 2.54% at night's beginning... Findings suggest "deeper sleep in the beginning of the night" with LD

claims.claim: This study measured no autonomic or heart-rate variables, so it cannot speak to wearable-tracked HRV/RHR effects of meal timing — a relevant gap when using it as evidence for a wearable-focused note.
claims.quote: The study measured no autonomic or heart rate measures.

claims.claim: A 48-hour total fast in healthy young women significantly reduced resting HRV (both SDNN and RMSSD) from baseline to 48h, indicating acute parasympathetic (vagal) withdrawal.
claims.quote: Significant decreases in SDNN and RMSSD from Day 1 to Day 3 (P<0.001)... acute (48 h) total fast induced parasympathetic withdrawal with simultaneous sympathetic activation

claims.claim: The acute 48h fast produced a shift toward sympathetic dominance (sympathovagal imbalance), evidenced by reduced RMSSD and log high-frequency power during head-up tilt testing.
claims.quote: Significant reductions in SDNN, RMSSD, and log high-frequency power (P<0.001)... simultaneous sympathetic activation

claims.claim: Contrary to a simple cortisol-driven stress response, diurnal cortisol shifted toward LOWER values by the end of the 48h fast.
claims.quote: Diurnal cortisol profile "significantly shifted towards lower values from baseline to the end" (P=0.002)

claims.claim: The study was small (16 healthy young female volunteers) and used a prolonged 48-hour total fast, limiting generalizability to typical overnight/16h time-restricted eating.
claims.quote: 16 healthy young female volunteers... 48 hours total, with measurements at baseline (Day 1), 24 hours (Day 2), and 48 hours (Day 3)

claims.claim: A systematic review of 6 RCTs (548 enrolled, 430 completers) found that short-to-mid-term TRE does not typically worsen sleep parameters, though effects were mixed and population-dependent.
claims.quote: short to mid-term TRE does not typically worsen sleep parameters

claims.claim: Habitual TRE effects on sleep quality/duration were inconsistent: only one study showed improved subjective sleep quality, while others found decreased sleep duration, decreased sleep efficiency (2 studies), or increased sleep onset latency.
claims.quote: Only one study reported significant improvements in subjective sleep quality

claims.claim: Meal-timing matters: late TRE (12pm-8pm) produced a ~2.7% decrease in objective sleep efficiency, while early TRE (7am-3pm) decreased self-reported PSQI sleep efficiency and increased sleep onset latency.
claims.quote: Late TRE (12pm-8pm): "significant decrease in mean sleep efficiency of 2.7%"

claims.claim: The evidence base is limited by short study durations (8-14 weeks) and few objective assessments, so long-term TRE effects on sleep cannot be concluded; no study measured REM/deep sleep architecture and hunger's effect on sleep was not addressed.
claims.quote: studies included in this review had a relatively short duration, ranging from 8 to 14 weeks, thus the long-term effects of TRE on sleep parameters cannot be concluded from this review

claims.claim: Populations studied were mostly adults with overweight or obesity (4 of 6 studies), plus one young-adult and one shift-worker study, mean ages 22-49; five of six studies were low risk of bias.
claims.quote: Four studies: "adults with overweight or obesity"

claims.claim: In a 10-week randomized crossover trial, only early TRE (eating 8am-4pm) — not late TRE (1pm-9pm) — significantly improved actigraphy-estimated sleep quality in 31 women with overweight/obesity, increasing sleep efficiency (p=0.047), decreasing awakening length (p=0.043), and lowering the sleep fragmentation index (p=0.029) within-group.
claims.quote: Sleep efficiency increased within eTRE (p = 0.047)... Awakening length decreased within eTRE (p = 0.043)... Sleep fragmentation index declined within eTRE (p = 0.029)... Late TRE showed no significant improvements

claims.claim: The sleep benefits of early TRE appeared only on objective actigraphy measures, not subjective ones: neither early nor late TRE changed the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index or self-reported sleep ratings, and no between-intervention (early vs late) differences were statistically detected.
claims.quote: No changes detected with either intervention using Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index or self-reported ratings

claims.claim: Sleep duration did not change under either early or late TRE, indicating the timing benefit was on sleep quality/efficiency rather than total sleep time.
claims.quote: no change in sleep duration was observed within both TRE interventions

claims.claim: Hunger did not differ between early and late TRE, and hunger/satiety showed no association with any sleep-quality metric, arguing against hunger being the mechanism linking meal timing to sleep.
claims.quote: We observed no differences between eTRE and lTRE in desire to eat, hunger, satiety, or perceived capacity to eat and no associations of hunger and satiety with any assessed sleep quality metric.

claims.claim: In a 12-week RCT (secondary analysis) of 20 adults with overweight/obesity, self-selected TRE produced no significant change in objectively measured sleep duration or quality versus non-TRE, with both groups averaging ~6.3 hours (insufficient) throughout.
claims.quote: No significant changes in objectively measured sleep between groups (average ~6.3 hours both periods)

claims.claim: Greater restriction of the eating window was associated with longer sleep duration at end of intervention (β = −0.46, p = 0.03), suggesting tighter TRE may modestly benefit sleep length even when group-level effects are null.
claims.quote: Greater eating window restriction associated with longer sleep at end-intervention (β = −0.46, p = 0.03)

claims.claim: TRE significantly reduced late-night eating from 36±13% to 14±6% of days (p = 0.028), and 63% of TRE participants completely eliminated eating within 2 hours of bedtime, while non-TRE showed no significant change (~43%).
claims.quote: TRE group significantly reduced late-night eating from 36±13% to 14±6% (p = 0.028)

claims.claim: At baseline, more frequent late-night eating correlated with worse metabolic markers — higher fasting glucose (r = 0.59, p = 0.006) and higher HbA1c (r = 0.46, p = 0.016).
claims.quote: At baseline, late-night eating correlated with higher fasting glucose (r = 0.59, p = 0.006) and HbA1c (r = 0.46, p = 0.016)

claims.claim: TRE shifted meal timing by delaying the first eating occasion 2.72±1.48 hours after wake (p<0.001) and advancing the last eating occasion 1.25±0.8 hours before bedtime (p<0.001), quantifying how a self-selected eating window changes meal timing.
claims.quote: TRE group delayed first eating occasion by 2.72±1.48 hours relative to wake (p < 0.001)

claims.claim: Long-term fasting (12-day Buchinger protocol, ~250 kcal/day) HABITUALLY raised parasympathetic/vagal tone: overnight RMSSD rose significantly from 27.16±10.5 to 32.92±17.65 ms (p=0.01) after the fasting period versus before.
claims.quote: RMSSD significantly increased from 27.16 ± 10.5 to 32.92 ± 17.65 ms

claims.claim: Sympathetic nervous system activity was biphasic across fasting: an initial sympathetic activation in the early fasting phase (p<0.05), followed by a significant decrease in the SNS index after fasting (p=0.00007).
claims.quote: Decreased after fasting" (p = 0.00007)... Early fasting phase showed initial sympathetic activation (p < 0.05)

claims.claim: Resting heart rate DECREASED after the fasting intervention (62.79 to 58.44 bpm, p<0.001), but during the fast itself heart rate showed only a slight, non-significant increase (67.2 to 69.2 bpm, p=0.52) — an acute-vs-habitual distinction.
claims.quote: Mean HR decreased post-fasting: 62.79 to 58.44 bpm (p < 0.001)... Slight non-significant increase during fasting: 67.2 to 69.2 bpm (p = 0.52)

claims.claim: The evidence is weak/preliminary: this was a single-arm (uncontrolled) interventional trial with only 16 participants (8M/8F, age 45±11, BMI 26±4), so causal claims about fasting's autonomic benefits require larger randomized studies.
claims.quote: Study authors acknowledge small sample size; larger randomized studies recommended for confirmation.

claims.claim: Self-reported sleep quality did not change over the 12-day fast despite the caloric restriction, while mental well-being improved significantly (p=0.029).
claims.quote: Improved significantly (p = 0.029)... Sleep quality remained unchanged

claims.claim: An acute fast increased vagally-mediated HRV in healthy young adults: R-R intervals rose from 992±30 to 1,059±37 ms and normalized high-frequency spectral power rose from 55±3% to 62±3%, indicating higher parasympathetic (vagal) tone during fasting.
claims.quote: R-R intervals increased from 992±30 to 1,059±37 ms; normalized high-frequency spectral power rose from 55±3 to 62±3%

claims.claim: An acute fast lowered resting heart rate from 69±2 to 65±2 beats/minute in healthy young normotensive volunteers.
claims.quote: Resting heart rate reduced from 69±2 to 65±2 beats/minute after fasting

claims.claim: Acute fasting did not significantly change muscle sympathetic nerve activity (16±11 vs. 15±8 bursts/minute), so the autonomic shift during fasting was driven by increased vagal tone rather than reduced sympathetic outflow.
claims.quote: Sympathetic Activity: No significant change (16±11 vs. 15±8 bursts/minute)

claims.claim: Acute fasting improved cardiovagal baroreflex sensitivity from 20±2 to 26±5 ms/mmHg and lowered mean arterial pressure from 81±1 to 78±1 mmHg.
claims.quote: Cardiovagal baroreflex sensitivity improved from 20±2 to 26±5 ms/mmHg... Mean arterial pressure decreased from 81±1 to 78±1 mmHg when fasted

claims.claim: Evidence base: this was a randomized crossover controlled trial in 25 healthy young normotensive volunteers (20 for BP, 23 for baroreflex, 12 for muscle sympathetic nerve activity), a small single-population sample.
claims.quote: Randomized controlled trial with crossover design... 25 young normotensive volunteers (20 for blood pressure analysis, 23 for baroreflex sensitivity, 12 for muscle sympathetic nerve activity)

claims.claim: In a 12-day supervised fast (~250 kcal/day, Buchinger protocol), parasympathetic tone (HRV RMSSD) rose significantly from 27.16±10.5 ms before fasting to 32.92±17.65 ms after (p<0.001) in 16 adults, indicating habitual/prolonged fasting increases vagal activity.
claims.quote: Pre-fasting: 27.16±10.5 ms; Post-fasting: 32.92±17.65 ms (p<0.001)

claims.claim: Sympathetic nervous system activity (SNS index) decreased significantly over the 12-day fast (p=0.00007), shifting sympatho-vagal balance toward parasympathetic dominance after prolonged fasting.
claims.quote: Sympathetic Activity (SNS Index): Decreased significantly (p=0.00007)

claims.claim: The autonomic response to fasting is biphasic: an initial acute rise in sympathetic activation occurs in the early fasting phase (p<0.05) before parasympathetic enhancement dominates, distinguishing acute from habitual effects.
claims.quote: an initial rise in sympathetic activation during the early fasting phase (p<0.05), followed by sustained parasympathetic enhancement during food reintroduction
